content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian interpretation, something 'cast into the sea' symbolizes complete, final, and irreversible removal or destruction. The sea functions as a place of no return: what sinks into it is gone forever. This core idea is applied in two directions: (a) irrevocable divine judgment — the violent, total overthrow of the wicked or of a wicked system (the millstone drowning warning; Babylon hurled like a millstone into the sea); and (b) irrevocable removal of an obstacle or of sin — faith removing 'mountains' of impossibility, and God casting sins into the depths of the sea so they can never be retrieved. The common thread taught across pulpits, commentaries, and study Bibles is finality and totality: whatever is cast into the sea is decisively done away with.","primary_basis":["Matthew 18:6 / Mark 9:42 / Luke 17:2 (better to have a millstone hung around the neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea than to cause a little one to stumble — severe, decisive judgment)","Matthew 21:21 / Mark 11:23 (say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and cast into the sea' — faith removing an immovable obstacle)","Luke 17:6 (the mulberry/sycamine tree uprooted and planted in the sea by mustard-seed faith)","Revelation 18:21 (a mighty angel throws a great millstone into the sea: 'so shall Babylon be thrown down with violence, and shall be found no more' — final, irreversible destruction)","Micah 7:19 (God will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea — total, unrecoverable forgiveness)","Exodus 15:1–5 / Nehemiah 9:11 (Pharaoh's army cast into the sea, sinking like a stone/lead — judgment as sinking without recovery)","Jonah 1:15; 2:3 (Jonah cast into the sea — being given over to judgment/the deep)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Faith accomplishing the impossible: the mountain or tree cast into the sea is read primarily as a hyperbolic image of prayer and faith overcoming insurmountable obstacles, rather than as judgment imagery.","basis":["Matthew 17:20","Matthew 21:21–22","Mark 11:22–24","Luke 17:6","1 Corinthians 13:2 ('faith so as to remove mountains')"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"Warning of divine judgment worse than death for causing believers ('little ones') to stumble: drowning with a millstone is a picture of the severity of God's judgment on those who lead others into sin.","basis":["Matthew 18:6","Mark 9:42","Luke 17:1–2"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"Complete forgiveness of sin: God burying sins in the depths of the sea signifies that forgiven sin is permanently removed and will never be brought up again ('sea of forgetfulness' in popular devotional usage).","basis":["Micah 7:19","Psalm 103:12 (paired thematically)","Isaiah 38:17"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Preterist/typological reading: 'this mountain' cast into the sea refers to the Temple Mount or the Jewish nation/old covenant order being judged and removed in AD 70; more broadly, a 'mountain' as a kingdom being overthrown into the 'sea' of the nations.","basis":["Mark 11:23 read against its Temple context (Mark 11:12–21)","Jeremiah 51:25, 42 (Babylon as a 'destroying mountain'; the sea coming up over Babylon)","Zechariah 4:7","Revelation 8:8 (a great mountain burning with fire thrown into the sea)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The sea as chaos, the abyss, or the Gentile nations: being cast into the sea means being consigned to the realm of chaos/death or dispersed among hostile nations, drawing on ancient Near Eastern chaos-waters imagery.","basis":["Revelation 8:8","Revelation 13:1; 21:1 ('the sea was no more')","Psalm 46:2","Isaiah 17:12–13","Daniel 7:2–3"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Deliverance through judgment on enemies: casting into the sea recalls the Exodus pattern — God destroying oppressors in the waters to save his people — so the image evokes salvation-through-judgment typology (sometimes linked to baptism).","basis":["Exodus 14–15","Nehemiah 9:11","1 Corinthians 10:1–2","Isaiah 43:16–17"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"medium","notes":"The confidence is medium rather than high because 'cast into the sea' is a composite term spanning several distinct passages (millstone, mountain, tree, Babylon, sins), and interpretive tradition treats each passage in its own frame: faith texts are read devotionally about prayer, millstone texts about judgment, Micah about forgiveness. However, the underlying symbolic logic — the sea as the place of total, irreversible disappearance, whether in judgment or in the removal of sin/obstacles — is broadly shared and recognizable across Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox commentary. No single unified 'cast into the sea' doctrine exists as a formal category, but the finality/irreversibility meaning is the closest thing to consensus. The preterist Temple-Mount reading and the chaos/nations reading are genuinely different frameworks held by identifiable minorities (preterist interpreters; scholars emphasizing ANE cosmology and apocalyptic symbolism)."}
